analysis.one_liner: Requires federal housing grant recipients to report what they're doing about restrictive local zoning.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee in May 2023 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require cities and counties that receive federal Community Development Block Grant money to periodically tell the Department of Housing and Urban Development whether they have adopted — or plan to adopt — a list of 22 zoning and land-use reforms, such as allowing duplexes in single-family neighborhoods, permitting apartments near transit, cutting parking mandates, and speeding up permits. Cities would not be forced to change anything; they would only have to report where they stand. The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and died there without any vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters and first-time homebuyers in cities with restrictive zoning, where rules that limit most residential land to one house per lot have been shown to raise housing costs. Tenants in high-cost metro areas would benefit if the reporting nudges cities toward allowing more homes, and the public would gain a standardized window into which local governments keep restrictive rules. Homebuilders and developers also stand to gain from expanded building opportunities.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Renters and first-time buyers in high-cost cities

how_it_helps.text: Requires certain Community Development Block Grant recipients to report to HUD, at least once every five years, whether they have adopted, plan to adopt, or how they would benefit from 22 land-use policies including high-density zoning, by-right multifamily housing, duplexes in single-family zones, smaller minimum lot sizes, transit-oriented development zones, streamlined permitting, reduced parking requirements, and accessory dwelling units [S3][S2].

The stated purpose is to discourage discriminatory land use policies and remove barriers to making housing more affordable, furthering the original intent of the Community Development Block Grant program [S3].

Creates a standardized public record of which jurisdictions keep restrictive zoning, giving residents and prospective movers information about local housing barriers that is currently scattered or unavailable [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Local governments that receive block grants would bear the paperwork cost of preparing standardized land-use reports. Incumbent homeowners and local officials who rely on restrictive zoning to limit new construction would face federal disclosure of their rules, though nothing in the bill forces a change. Developers of large greenfield subdivisions gain relatively less than builders of infill housing.
analysis.who_pays_short: Grant-receiving local governments and zoning-status-quo defenders

drawbacks.text: The requirement has no enforcement teeth: a submission 'shall not be binding with respect to the use or distribution of amounts received,' and HUD's acceptance or rejection of a plan is explicitly not an endorsement, so a city can file paperwork and change nothing [S3].

Defenders of local control — a position held across both parties for land-use decisions — object to Washington pressuring cities on zoning, an area traditionally governed by states and municipalities; the reporting mandate is a federal foot in the door even if soft [S3].

Housing advocates can reasonably say a once-every-five-years questionnaire will not lower rents on its own, since the bill provides no money, no mandate, and no consequence for jurisdictions that adopt none of the 22 policies [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct cost is small — paperwork for grant recipients — and the direct benefit is also small, since the bill changes no rules and withholds no money. Its real value is informational and incremental: it would create a public, standardized record of which cities block housing and nudge recipients toward the zoning reforms that research links to lower housing costs. It is a transparency step, not a housing solution, and anyone expecting it to materially cut rents would be disappointed.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee in May 2023, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025 [S5][S1].

narrative.text: Sen. Todd Young (R-IN), with Sen. Brian Schatz (D-HI), introduced the Yes In My Backyard Act on May 18, 2023 [S1][S3].
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs; no further action was recorded for the remainder of the Congress [S5].
Seven senators cosponsored the bill — 4 of 48 Senate Democrats and 3 of 49 Senate Republicans — giving it bipartisan sponsorship, but it never reached a committee vote or a floor vote [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because nothing happened, the status quo held: local governments face no federal reporting on their zoning, and officials and homeowners who benefit from restrictive land-use rules face no added disclosure. Renters and buyers in high-cost cities gained nothing, and neither did builders who would have welcomed more permissive rules. With a low-cost, non-binding bill, the main effect of its death is that a modest transparency tool was never built.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Zoning status quo; no new reporting for cities

for.name: Sen. Todd Young
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate Banking Committee on May 18, 2023.

for.name: Sen. Brian Schatz
for.role: Original cosponsor, named in the introduction
for.what_they_did: Joined Sen. Young in introducing the bill, providing bipartisan sponsorship from the start.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Sherrod Brown, D-OH)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, and no vote in the 20 months before the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader
against.role: Senate floor scheduler (Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-NY)
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; a bill cannot get a vote without the leader scheduling one, and none was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had sponsors and cosponsors from both parties from day one — a Republican lead sponsor, a Democratic original cosponsor, and 7 cosponsors split 4 Democrats to 3 Republicans — and died in committee with no recorded opposition vote rather than along party lines [S3][S4][S5].

industries.note: If the reporting nudges cities toward allowing duplexes, apartments, and faster permits, builders get more places to build, and the added supply serves renters and buyers facing high prices. The industry's interest here runs alongside the public's, though the bill's reporting-only design means any gain is indirect.

Restrictive single-family zoning protects the value of existing homes by limiting competing supply, so disclosure of which cities keep those rules is a cost to homeowners who rely on scarcity. They are not forced to change anything, but the bill would shine a standardized light on the rules that keep housing scarce for everyone else.

industries.industry: Local governments receiving Community Development Block Grants
industries.note: Grant recipients would face a new reporting obligation every five years but would keep full control of their grant money, since submissions are explicitly non-binding. The burden is administrative, and no funding is at stake.
